set1.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set1.q: Guests at one banquet eat a contaminated dish, and all of their exposure falls within a single incubation period. Which type of epidemic is this?
opts: Propagated
A propagated epidemic spreads person to person; a single shared meal is a common point source.
Mixed
A mixed epidemic starts from a common source and then spreads person to person; a single brief exposure is a point source.
Common source, point
Correct: a common source epidemic exposes a group to the same source; when exposure is brief, within one incubation period, it is a point source.
Common source, continuous
A continuous common source exposes people over a longer time; one brief exposure within an incubation period is a point source.

set1.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set1.q: A single survey finds that people who report a certain exposure have more of a disease than people who do not, and nothing more is known. How is this relationship best classed?
opts: An association
Correct: an identifiable relationship between an exposure and a disease is an association; it implies the exposure might cause the disease, but finding an association does not make it causal.
Causation
Causation implies a true mechanism that leads from exposure to disease; one survey showing a relationship is an association, and finding an association does not make it causal.
A biological gradient
A biological gradient is a dose-response relationship, where changes in exposure track a trend in risk; a plain exposed-versus-unexposed comparison shows no such trend.
A temporal sequence
Temporal sequence means the exposure is shown to come before the disease; nothing here shows which came first, so the finding is an association.

mis.A biological gradient: Hill criterion confused with the finding
mis.A temporal sequence: Hill criterion confused with the finding

set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 43 and 46

set1.io: 4 — Identify common sources of epidemiologic data
set1.q: Air-quality ratings collected by sensors are which source of epidemiologic data?
opts: Nonhealth-related sources
Nonhealth-related sources are financial and legal records; air-quality sensor data are environmental.
The environment
Correct: the environment supplies data through samples and sensors for environmental changes, including air-quality ratings.
Individual persons
Individual persons are surveyed or given questionnaires; sensor readings of air quality are environmental data.
Health care providers
Providers notify the health department of cases of certain diseases; air-quality ratings come from the environment.

set1.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set1.q: Which type of surveillance uses staff members to contact health care providers regularly for data?
opts: Sentinel surveillance
Sentinel surveillance relies on a prearranged group that agrees to report all cases; staff phoning providers regularly is active surveillance.
Active surveillance
Correct: active surveillance uses staff to regularly contact providers; it is the most accurate but the most expensive, and often used during outbreaks or seasonal events.
Passive surveillance
Passive surveillance waits for reports submitted by facilities and providers; regularly contacting providers is active surveillance.
Syndromic surveillance
Syndromic surveillance is defined by case definitions based on clinical features alone; staff contacting providers is active surveillance.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 19 and 20

set1.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set1.q: Which critical characteristic of surveillance allows individual persons with disease to be identified for treatment or quarantine?
opts: Timeliness
Timeliness lets control measures be implemented effectively; identifying individual persons with disease is sensitivity.
Representation
Representation gives an accurate picture of the disease's temporal trend; identifying individual cases is sensitivity.
Sensitivity
Correct: sensitivity allows identification of individual persons with disease, to facilitate treatment, quarantine or other control measures.
Specificity
Specificity excludes persons who do not have the disease; finding the persons who do have it is sensitivity.

set1.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set1.q: Three studies each find that lung cancer mortality rises steadily from fewer than 10 to more than 40 cigarettes a day. Which of Hill's criteria does this rising trend most directly support?
opts: Specificity
Specificity is an exposure leading to a single or characteristic effect; a risk that climbs with dose is the biological gradient.
Temporal sequence
Temporal sequence asks whether exposure came first; a risk rising with each step in dose is the biological gradient.
Plausibility
Plausibility asks whether the mechanism makes biological sense; a stepwise rise with dose is the biological gradient.
Biological gradient
Correct: a trend in risk with increasing dose, here more cigarettes per day, is a dose-response relationship, the biological gradient.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 49 and image on Slide 49

set1.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set1.q: What is the first step in investigating a communicable disease outbreak?
opts: Verify the diagnosis
Verifying the diagnosis comes third, after establishing the outbreak and preparing for field work.
Develop a focused hypothesis
A focused hypothesis comes after cases are defined and described with descriptive epidemiology.
Implement control measures
Control and prevention measures come near the end, after the hypothesis is evaluated and refined.
Establish its existence
Correct: the investigation begins by establishing the existence of an outbreak, then preparing for field work and verifying the diagnosis.

set1.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set1.q: A survey asks every adult in a town whether they currently have asthma, and those answering yes are divided by the town's adults. What is it measuring?
opts: Attack rate
An attack rate is the proportion of an exposed group falling ill in an outbreak; current cases in a survey is prevalence.
Prevalence
Correct: all cases present at or during a time period, over the population, is prevalence; a survey of who currently has a condition measures it.
Incidence
Incidence counts only new cases arising in a period; asking who currently has asthma counts all cases present, which is prevalence.
Crude mortality
Crude mortality counts deaths from all causes; current cases over the population is prevalence.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 27 and 28

set1.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set1.q: Where does case surveillance begin?
opts: Hospital billing offices
Billing is not part of case surveillance; it begins with local and state public health departments collecting data on cases.
Community health surveys
Surveys collect data from individual persons; case surveillance begins with local and state health departments collecting data about cases.
Local and state health departments

Correct: case surveillance begins with local and state public health departments collecting data about cases; notifiable conditions are then reported on to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention receives notifiable cases after local and state health departments collect them; the process begins locally.

set1.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set1.q: A relative risk that is either very high or very low is less likely to be due to chance or bias. Which of Hill's criteria is this?
opts: Strength of association
Correct: a strong association is one in which the relative risk is either very high or very low, and it is less likely to be caused by chance or bias.
Consistency of findings
Consistency is the same result across multiple studies and populations; a very high or very low relative risk is strength.
Biological gradient
Biological gradient is a trend in relative risk across doses; a single very high or very low relative risk is strength of association.
Temporal sequence
Temporal sequence is exposure preceding disease; a very high or very low relative risk is strength of association.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 46 and 48

set1.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set1.q: In the host-agent-environment triad, which of these is a host factor?
opts: Crowded housing
Living conditions such as crowding belong to the environment, not the host.
A biting vector
A vector is one of the environment's modes of communication that bring host and agent together.
A dietary allergen
Allergens are listed among the agents (environmental agents); immunologic status is a host factor.
Immunologic status
Correct: host factors are genetic endowment, immunologic status, personal characteristics, personal behavior, and definitive versus intermediate host in vector-borne disease.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 38, 39 and 40

set1.io: 6 — Define reportable disease
set1.q: What does collecting reportable disease data allow authorities to do?
opts: Monitor disease, warn of outbreaks
Correct: data collection lets authorities monitor the disease and provides early warning of potential outbreaks.
Prove what causes each disease
Reports monitor disease and warn of outbreaks; epidemiology infers causation from association and other factors, and does not prove the cause of each disease.
Bill patients for public testing
Billing is not the purpose; reportable disease data let authorities monitor disease and get early warning of outbreaks.
Replace physicians' diagnoses
Reports depend on diagnoses rather than replacing them; their purpose is monitoring and early warning of outbreaks.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 21 and 43

set1.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set1.q: How was the bacterium behind the 1976 Legionnaires' disease epidemic finally found?
opts: A doctor isolated it on the first weekend
The health department was closed that weekend; the bacterium was located in December 1976 by persistent testing of specimens thought to be dead.
A survey of residents identified it
Surveys identify exposures, not organisms; the bacterium was found by a laboratorian who kept testing specimens thought to be dead.
Genomic sequencing matched the cases
Genomic epidemiology monitors the genetic makeup of pathogens; this bacterium was found by persistent laboratory testing of specimens thought to be dead.
Testing of specimens thought dead
Correct: in December 1976, a laboratorian at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention located the source bacteria by continuing to test specimens that were thought to be dead.

mis.A survey of residents identified it: descriptive tool confused with laboratory method

set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 64, 68 and 69

set1.io: 3 — Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology, including genomic epidemiology
set1.q: Who is called the father of modern vital statistics?
opts: John Snow
John Snow is called the father of field epidemiology, for his work on the London cholera epidemic; Farr is the father of modern vital statistics.
John Graunt
John Graunt pioneered tabulating mortality as rates and ratios in the 17th century; the father of modern vital statistics is William Farr.
Hippocrates
Hippocrates explained disease rationally through environmental and host factors; modern vital statistics began with William Farr.
William Farr
Correct: William Farr systematically collected and analyzed Britain's mortality statistics in the 1800s, developed life-table approaches and reported his findings to authorities and the public.

set1.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set1.q: How are most diseases caused?
opts: By microbes alone
Microbes are one strand of the web; most diseases are caused by an interplay of factors including genes, environment and behavior.
By genes alone
Genes are one strand of the web of causation; most diseases are caused by an interplay of different factors.
By an interplay of factors
Correct: a cause is not generally a single factor; most diseases are caused by an interplay of different factors, a web of genes, microbes, environment, behavior and more.
By one necessary factor
A single factor is not the general rule; most diseases arise from an interplay of different factors.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 45 and image on Slide 45

set1.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set1.q: What is a map marking where each person with a disease lived and worked called?
opts: An epidemic curve
An epidemic curve plots cases by date of onset; a map of where cases lived and worked is a spot map.
A surveillance indicator
An indicator is a measurable factor that estimates the size of a health problem; marking each case's home and workplace is a spot map.
An attack-rate table
An attack-rate table tabulates the ill among the exposed; marking cases on a map is a spot map.
A spot map
Correct: marking where persons with cholera lived and worked, as John Snow did, makes what is now called a spot map.

set1.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set1.q: For a chronic disease such as osteoarthritis, which has a long duration and an onset date that is hard to pinpoint, which measure is usually used?
opts: Prevalence
Correct: prevalence rather than incidence is often measured for chronic diseases such as diabetes or osteoarthritis, which have long duration and hard-to-pinpoint onset.
Incidence
Incidence needs the onset of each new case to be dated; for long chronic diseases with vague onset, prevalence is measured instead.
Case fatality rate
The case fatality rate measures deaths among cases; for chronic disease burden with vague onset, prevalence is used.
Attack rate
An attack rate describes the ill among the exposed in an outbreak; chronic diseases with vague onset are measured by prevalence.

set1.io: 3 — Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology, including genomic epidemiology
set1.q: What is genomic epidemiology?
opts: Monitoring the genetic makeup of pathogens
Correct: genomic epidemiology is the process of monitoring the genetic makeup of the pathogens that cause disease, made possible by advances in sequencing.
Tracing inherited disease in families
Genomic epidemiology studies the pathogens' genes, not inherited human disease; it monitors the genetic makeup of disease-causing pathogens.
Testing new vaccines in clinical trials
Evaluating vaccine and clinical trials is program evaluation; genomic epidemiology monitors the genetic makeup of pathogens.
Mapping cases by home and workplace
Mapping where cases lived and worked is a spot map, descriptive epidemiology; genomic epidemiology monitors pathogens' genetic makeup.

mis.Tracing inherited disease in families: human genetics confused with pathogen genomics

set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 12 and 69

set1.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set1.q: A prearranged group of providers agrees to report every case of a condition, tracking it for a much larger population. Which type of surveillance is this?
opts: Sentinel surveillance
Correct: sentinel surveillance uses a prearranged group of reporting sources, usually providers, as a smaller representative group tracking on behalf of a larger population.
Passive surveillance
Passive surveillance relies on whatever reports facilities submit; a prearranged group agreeing to report all cases is sentinel surveillance.
Active surveillance
Active surveillance sends staff to contact providers regularly; a prearranged reporting group is sentinel surveillance.
Syndromic surveillance
Syndromic surveillance is defined by case definitions based on clinical features alone; a prearranged representative group is sentinel.

set1.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set1.q: An infection spreads from person to person through a community. Which type of epidemic is this?
opts: Common source, continuous
A continuous common source exposes people to the same source over a longer time; person-to-person spread is propagated.
Endemic
Endemic describes chronically low levels, not a type of epidemic; person-to-person spread is a propagated epidemic.
Propagated
Correct: a propagated epidemic is person-to-person transmission, reflecting spreading infection that may be extended.
Common source, point
A point source exposes a group to one source over a short time; person-to-person spread is propagated.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 36 and 55

set1.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set1.q: Which three phenomena are assessed in analytic epidemiology?
opts: Exposure, latency and outcome
Latency belongs to the temporal-sequence criterion for causation; the analytic triad is host, agent and environment.
Host, agent and environment
Correct: the basic triad of analytic epidemiology is host, agent and environment.
Person, place and time
Person, place and time are the triad of descriptive epidemiology, understood first; analytic epidemiology assesses host, agent and environment.
Sensitivity, specificity and timeliness
These are critical characteristics of surveillance; analytic epidemiology assesses host, agent and environment.

set1.io: 2 — Describe the specific uses for epidemiology training
set1.q: Among the five W's of epidemiology, which one names the health event or diagnosis?
opts: Who
Who is the person or population involved; the health event or diagnosis is What.
Where
Where is the location of the event; the health event or diagnosis itself is What.
Why
Why covers the causes, risk factors and modes of transmission; the health event or diagnosis is What.
What
Correct: What is the health event or diagnosis; Who is the person or population, Where the location, When the time period and Why the causes.

set1.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set1.q: In 1994, what change in approach to youth smoking did the Surgeon General's report recommend?
opts: Leave the issue to individual families
The report moved away from individual-level focus toward a community and population approach.
Concentrate efforts on adult smokers
Adult smoking had already fallen by the 1980s; the report addressed youth smoking as a community and population issue.
Treat it as a community and population issue
Correct: the report recommended moving from campaigns focused on individual young people to addressing youth smoking as a community and population issue.
Focus campaigns on individual young people
That was the approach being replaced; the report recommended treating youth smoking as a community and population issue.

set1.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set1.q: Which measure counts only the new cases that arise during a given time period?
opts: Crude mortality rate
The crude mortality rate counts deaths from all causes; counting new cases is incidence.
Incidence
Correct: the numerator of incidence is the new cases that occurred during the time period; incidence is likened to a speedometer.
Prevalence
The numerator of prevalence is all cases present during the period, old and new; only new cases is incidence.
Case fatality rate
The case fatality rate is deaths divided by total cases; counting new cases is incidence.

set1.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set1.q: Epidemiological studies can bring about major health policy changes when they meet which condition?
opts: Paired with matching political support
Politics is one basis of policy alongside values, ideology and evidence; a study's own route to policy change is being rigorously conducted, reported and communicated.
Rigorously done, reported and communicated

Correct: epidemiological studies can result in major health policy changes if they are rigorously conducted, reported and communicated; the evidence they supply is epidemiology's main contribution to policy.
Large enough to include every resident
Studies sample the population rather than count everyone; what lets a study change policy is being rigorously conducted, reported and communicated.
Approved by the affected communities
Community approval is not the condition; studies change policy when rigorously conducted, reported and communicated, adding evidence to the values, ideology and politics behind policy.

set1.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set1.q: Which branch of epidemiology examines how a disease is distributed in a population by time, place and person?
opts: Genomic epidemiology
Genomic epidemiology monitors pathogens' genetic makeup; the time-place-person description of a disease is descriptive epidemiology.
Experimental epidemiology
Experimental epidemiology tests a hypothesis with an experimental model; describing distribution is descriptive epidemiology.
Descriptive epidemiology
Correct: descriptive epidemiology examines a disease's distribution in terms of time, place and person, and uses it to formulate hypotheses.
Analytic epidemiology
Analytic epidemiology tests a specific hypothesis relating an exposure to an outcome; describing distribution by time, place and person is descriptive.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 32 and 33

set1.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set1.q: What is a pandemic?
opts: A worldwide epidemic
Correct: pandemics are diseases that are worldwide epidemics.
A disease at low, steady levels
A disease found at chronically low levels in a population is endemic; a pandemic is a worldwide epidemic.
An isolated, irregular case
Isolated incidents at irregular intervals are sporadic; a pandemic is a worldwide epidemic.
A disease reported by law
A disease required by law to be reported is notifiable; a pandemic is a worldwide epidemic.

set1.io: 2 — Describe the specific uses for epidemiology training
set1.q: Which use of epidemiological training develops a hypothesis for a health concern and designs an experimental model to test it?
opts: Experimental epidemiology
Correct: experimental epidemiology develops a hypothesis for a health concern and designs an experimental model to test it.
Program evaluation
Program evaluation and management assesses prevention and intervention programs such as vaccine and clinical trials; designing a model to test a hypothesis is experimental epidemiology.
Disease prioritization
Disease prioritization ranks diseases of concern by who gets them, who dies and the outcome; hypothesis testing by experiment is experimental epidemiology.
Public health surveillance
Surveillance work is setting up, managing and evaluating surveillance systems; designing an experimental model is experimental epidemiology.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 7 and 8

set1.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set1.q: What is herd immunity?
opts: Antibody made after a single infection
Antibody after infection is one person's acquired resistance; herd immunity measures how many in the population are immune.
The share of a population that is immune
Correct: herd immunity is the cumulative number of immune persons in a population, or the percentage of the population that is immune.
Resistance one person inherits from parents
Inherited resistance is one route to an individual's immunity; herd immunity is the number or percentage of immune persons in a population.
A vaccine given to every member of a herd
Vaccination contributes to herd immunity but is not its definition; herd immunity is the number or share of immune persons in a population.

set1.io: 3 — Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology, including genomic epidemiology
set1.q: Which 17th-century figure pioneered tabulating population health and mortality as rates, ratios and proportions?
opts: Doll and Hill
Doll and Hill linked smoking and lung cancer in 1950; the 17th-century pioneer of mortality tables was John Graunt.
John Graunt

Correct: John Graunt pioneered tabulating population health and mortality in rates, ratios and proportions, noting male-female differences, high infant mortality, urban-rural differences and seasonal variation.
William Farr
William Farr worked in the 1800s, analyzing Britain's mortality statistics; the 17th-century pioneer of tabulation was John Graunt.
Hippocrates
Hippocrates, around 400 BC, explained disease through environmental and host factors; tabulating mortality as rates came with John Graunt.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 10 and 11

set2.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set2.q: What are exposures associated with a difference in disease risk often called?
opts: Vehicles
A vehicle is an environmental mode of communication bringing host and agent together; exposures linked to risk are risk factors.
Confounders
A confounded association is one level of the pyramid of associations; exposures associated with disease risk are called risk factors.
Risk factors
Correct: exposures associated with a difference in disease risk are often called risk factors.
Indicators
An indicator is a measurable factor estimating the size of a health problem; exposures linked to disease risk are risk factors.

set2.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set2.q: A surveillance system counts cases of diarrhea rather than laboratory-confirmed cholera. Which type of surveillance is this?
opts: Genomic surveillance
Genomic methods identify pathogens by their genetic makeup, the opposite of a clinical-feature definition; this is syndromic surveillance.
Syndromic surveillance
Correct: syndromic surveillance uses case definitions based entirely on clinical features, such as diarrhea instead of cholera; it is the system most often found in developing countries.
Sentinel surveillance
Sentinel surveillance is defined by a prearranged group of reporters, not by clinical case definitions; counting diarrhea instead of cholera is syndromic.
Active surveillance
Active surveillance is defined by staff contacting providers; using clinical features alone for the case definition is syndromic.

set2.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set2.q: Policy development rests on values, ideology, politics and evidence. Which of these is epidemiology's main contribution?
opts: Ideology
Ideology shapes policy too, but what epidemiology contributes is evidence.
Politics
Politics is one basis of policy development; epidemiology's main contribution is evidence.
Evidence
Correct: evidence is the main contribution of epidemiology to policy; it is not usually the main influence on policy, but it is worth fighting for.
Values
Values are one basis of policy development, but epidemiology's main contribution is evidence.

set2.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set2.q: Which three elements form the basic triad of descriptive epidemiology?
opts: Incidence, prevalence and mortality
Incidence, prevalence and mortality measure disease burden; the descriptive triad is person, place and time.
Person, place and time
Correct: person, place and time are the essential characteristics of a descriptive study, understood before any analytic study is undertaken.
Host, agent and environment
Host, agent and environment are the triad assessed in analytic epidemiology; the descriptive triad is person, place and time.
Who, what and why
These are three of the five W's of epidemiology; the descriptive triad is person, place and time.

set2.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set2.q: Across many studies in different populations, an exposure comes before a disease, risk rises steadily with the amount of exposure, and the mechanism fits what is known about the disease. What do these findings support?
opts: Chance alone
Chance is one level of the pyramid of associations, apart from a causal one; findings repeated across many studies, with a dose-response trend, meet Hill's criteria for inferring causation.
A spurious association

A spurious (artifact) association is another level of the pyramid of associations, apart from a causal one; consistent, dose-related, plausible findings that follow the exposure meet Hill's criteria for causation.
A confounded association

A confounded association is another level of the pyramid of associations, apart from a causal one; consistency, dose-response, temporal sequence and plausibility are the criteria for inferring causation.
Inferring causation
Correct: causation is inferred from an association plus other factors; consistency, a biological gradient, temporal sequence and plausibility are Hill's criteria for causal inference.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slides 43, 44, 46 and 49

set2.io: 3 — Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology, including genomic epidemiology
set2.q: In the 1960s and 1970s, epidemiological methods were applied to which worldwide achievement?
opts: Eradicating smallpox
Correct: in the 1960s and 1970s, epidemiological methods were applied to eradicate smallpox worldwide.
Eradicating cholera
Cholera was the subject of John Snow's 19th-century work; the worldwide eradication achieved in the 1960s and 1970s was of smallpox.
Eliminating tuberculosis
Tuberculosis remains a concern, including drug-resistant strains; the 1960s-1970s eradication was of smallpox.
Ending influenza outbreaks
Influenza keeps changing and remains a concern; the worldwide eradication achieved with epidemiological methods was smallpox.

mis.Eradicating cholera: adjacent disease from the same history

set2.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set2.q: In the host-agent-environment triad, tobacco is classed as which kind of agent?
opts: Biological
Biological agents are microorganisms; tobacco is listed with acids, alkalis and poisons as a chemical agent.
Physical
Physical agents are temperature, radiation and trauma; tobacco is a chemical agent.
Psychological
Psychological experiences are their own category; tobacco is a chemical agent alongside acids, alkalis and poisons.
Chemical
Correct: chemical agents include acids, alkalis, poisons and tobacco.

mis.Psychological: adjacent agent class (behavioral habit read as psychological)

set2.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set2.q: Findings repeated in multiple studies, across different populations, circumstances and study designs, satisfy which of Hill's criteria?
opts: Biological gradient
Biological gradient is a dose-response trend; agreement across studies, populations and designs is consistency.
Consistency of findings
Correct: consistency of findings is a result demonstrated in multiple studies, across different populations, in differing circumstances and with different study designs.
Strength of association
Strength is a very high or very low relative risk in a study; repetition across studies and populations is consistency.
Specificity of association
Specificity is an exposure leading to a single or characteristic effect; repetition across studies is consistency.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 46 and 47

set2.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set2.q: In John Snow's investigation of a London cholera outbreak, why did workers at a nearby brewery have few cases?
opts: They had been vaccinated against cholera
Vaccination played no part; the brewery workers took their water from the brewery's own deep well rather than Pump A.
They lived far outside the outbreak area
The brewery sat about two blocks east of Pump A, inside the area; its workers drank from its deep well instead.
They boiled their water before drinking it
No boiling is described; the brewery's employees got their water from its own deep well, not from Pump A.
They drew water from the brewery's deep well
Correct: the brewery had its own deep well and its employees were permitted to get their water there, so they avoided Pump A.

mis.They boiled their water before drinking: plausible lay belief not in the case

set2.io: 2 — Describe the specific uses for epidemiology training
set2.q: Among the five W's of epidemiology, what does 'Why' cover?
opts: The person or population involved
The person or population involved is Who; Why covers the causes, risk factors and modes of transmission.
The location of the health event
The location of the event is Where; Why asks about causes, risk factors and modes of transmission.
The time period of the health event
The time period of the event is When; Why asks about causes, risk factors and modes of transmission.
Causes, risks and transmission
Correct: Why covers the causes, risk factors and modes of transmission; What is the health event, Who the person or population, Where the location and When the time period.

set2.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set2.q: Besides vaccination, what else adds to herd immunity?
opts: Reporting cases to authorities
Reporting monitors disease and warns of outbreaks but immunizes no one; natural immunity after recovery adds to herd immunity.
Lowering the case fatality rate
The case fatality rate is deaths over cases; herd immunity grows with natural immunity after recovery as well as vaccination.
Recovery from the infection
Correct: herd immunity is often discussed with vaccination, and it is also impacted by natural immunity gained by recovery from the infection.
Treating cases with antibiotics
Treatment is not named as a source of immunity; herd immunity is impacted by natural immunity gained by recovering from the infection, as well as by vaccination.

set2.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set2.alt: A bar chart of hepatitis A cases by date of onset in November and December: one food handler case marked as the presumed index case in early November, then a single tall, sharp cluster of cases in late November with a smooth curve over it, and a few secondary cases afterward.
set2.slide: Epidemic curve: hepatitis A cases by date of onset.
set2.q: This epidemic curve shows hepatitis A cases after one food handler fell ill, rising to a single sharp peak. Which type of epidemic does it show?
opts: Common source, continuous
A continuous common source keeps exposing people over a longer time, giving a long, flat spread of cases; one sharp peak means a brief, point exposure.
Propagated
Propagated spread builds in successive waves from person to person; one sharp peak after a single source is a point common source.
Other, zoonotic
Zoonotic and vector-borne epidemics fall under 'other'; a single sharp peak traced to one food handler is a point common source.
Common source, point
Correct: the cases share one source and the exposure was brief, so they cluster into one sharp peak within about one incubation period: a point common source.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 55 and image on Slide 56

set2.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set2.q: Which term describes a disease that occurs at irregular intervals or as isolated incidents?
opts: Epidemic
An epidemic is an excess of cases over what is expected; isolated incidents are sporadic.
Pandemic
A pandemic is a worldwide epidemic; isolated, irregular incidents are sporadic.
Sporadic
Correct: sporadic diseases occur at irregular intervals or as isolated incidents.
Endemic
Endemic diseases are found at chronically low levels, a steady presence; isolated, irregular cases are sporadic.

set2.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set2.q: Which step of the public health approach asks what the cause of a problem is?
opts: Implementation
Implementation asks 'How do you do it?'; 'What is the cause?' is risk factor identification.
Risk factor identification

Correct: the public health approach runs surveillance (what is the problem?), risk factor identification (what is the cause?), intervention evaluation (what works?) and implementation (how do you do it?).
Surveillance
Surveillance asks 'What is the problem?'; 'What is the cause?' is risk factor identification.
Intervention evaluation
Intervention evaluation asks 'What works?'; 'What is the cause?' is risk factor identification.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 71 and image on Slide 71

set2.io: 6 — Define reportable disease
set2.q: Which notifiable disease is reported as a total number of cases rather than case by case?
opts: Chickenpox
Correct: chickenpox and influenza are in the group reported as a total number of cases.
Gonorrhea
Gonorrhea requires a mandatory written report; chickenpox and influenza are reported as total numbers.
Rubeola
Rubeola requires a mandatory report by telephone; chickenpox is reported as a total number of cases.
Pertussis
Pertussis requires a mandatory telephone report; chickenpox and influenza are reported as totals.

set2.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set2.alt: A bar chart of measles cases by day of onset from mid-October 1970 to mid-January 1971: scattered single cases, then a cluster in mid-November, a taller peak in early December and the tallest peak in mid-December, each wave following the last.
set2.slide: Epidemic curve: measles cases by day of onset.
set2.q: This epidemic curve shows measles cases by day of onset, with a series of successively larger waves. Which type of epidemic does it show?
opts: Common source, point
A point source gives one sharp peak within a single incubation period; repeated, growing waves show propagated spread.
Common source, continuous
A continuous common source gives cases spread over the period of exposure that stop when it is removed; successive growing waves show person-to-person spread.
Other, vector-borne
Vector-borne epidemics such as West Nile or Lyme fall under 'other'; measles waves building on each other show propagated spread.
Propagated
Correct: successive, growing waves of cases are the pattern of person-to-person (propagated) transmission, a spreading infection that may be extended.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 55 and image on Slide 57

set2.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set2.alt: A bar chart of diarrheal illness in city residents by date of onset from mid-December to mid-January, bloody and nonbloody cases stacked; arrows mark water main breaks in late December, a boil-water order in early January and chlorination later; cases rise over about two weeks and fall away after the boil-water order.
set2.slide: Epidemic curve: diarrheal illness in city residents by date of onset.
set2.q: This epidemic curve follows diarrheal illness in city residents for several weeks after water main breaks, falling away after a boil-water order. Which type of epidemic does it show?
opts: Common source, point
A point source is a brief exposure within one incubation period, giving one sharp peak; weeks of exposure to the water supply make it continuous.
Propagated
Propagated spread is person to person in successive waves; cases tied to the water supply over weeks are a continuous common source.
Sporadic
Sporadic describes isolated incidents at irregular intervals, not an epidemic curve of many linked cases; this is a continuous common source.
Common source, continuous
Correct: the residents shared one source, the water supply, over a longer time than one incubation period, so cases kept coming until the source was dealt with: a continuous common source.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 55 and image on Slide 56

set2.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set2.q: A new therapy keeps people with an incurable disease alive far longer, while the number of new cases each year stays the same. What happens to the disease's prevalence?
opts: It stays the same
Incidence is unchanged, but prevalence also depends on duration; longer survival without cure raises prevalence.
It equals incidence
Prevalence counts all cases present and incidence only new ones; with longer survival prevalence rises further above incidence.
It rises
Correct: prevalence depends on incidence and duration; prolonged survival without cure lengthens duration, so prevalence rises even with unchanged incidence.
It falls
Prevalence would fall with a rapidly fatal course or rapid recovery; longer survival without cure raises it.

set2.io: 3 — Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology, including genomic epidemiology
set2.q: Who is called the father of field epidemiology?
opts: John Graunt
John Graunt pioneered tabulating mortality as rates and ratios; field epidemiology traces to John Snow's cholera investigations.
John Snow
Correct: John Snow, an anesthesiologist, used epidemiologic approaches to understand the London cholera epidemic and is called the father of field epidemiology.
William Farr
William Farr is the father of modern vital statistics, for collecting and analyzing Britain's mortality data; field epidemiology's father is John Snow.
Robert Koch
Koch's postulates, published in 1884, link microbes causally to disease; the father of field epidemiology is John Snow, who worked without knowledge of microbes.

mis.Robert Koch: germ theory confused with field method

set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 11 and 42

set2.io: 4 — Identify common sources of epidemiologic data
set2.q: Water is collected from local streams to check for chemical pollutants. Which source of epidemiologic data is this?
opts: Health care providers
Providers notify the health department of certain diseases; stream water samples come from the environment.
Nonhealth-related sources
Nonhealth-related sources are sales and court records; water samples are environmental data.
The environment
Correct: environmental data come from samples (river water, soil) and sensors, such as checking stream water for chemical pollutants or air-quality ratings.
Individual persons
Individual persons supply data through questionnaires and surveys; stream samples are environmental data.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the specific uses for epidemiology training
set2.q: An epidemiologist describes who gets a disease, who dies from it and what its outcome is, to rank it against other diseases of concern. Which use of epidemiological training is this?
opts: Disease prioritization
Correct: disease prioritization evaluates and ranks diseases of concern, including describing the clinical picture: who gets the disease, who dies and what the outcome is.
Outbreak response
Outbreak response identifies, reports and investigates outbreaks in a timely way; ranking diseases by who gets them and who dies is prioritization.
Public health communication
Communication is developing and delivering public health messages; describing and ranking diseases of concern is disease prioritization.
Experimental epidemiology
Experimental epidemiology designs an experimental model to test a hypothesis; ranking diseases by their clinical picture is disease prioritization.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 7 and 8

set2.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set2.q: A county counts residents newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes during the past year and divides by the county's residents at midyear. What is it measuring?
opts: Incidence
Correct: new cases arising during a given period, over the population, is incidence; the numerator of incidence is new cases only.
Prevalence
Prevalence would count all residents who have diabetes, new and old; counting only the newly diagnosed measures incidence.
Cause-specific mortality
Cause-specific mortality counts deaths from a specific cause; this counts new diagnoses, which is incidence.
Case fatality rate
The case fatality rate is deaths over total cases; new diagnoses over the population is incidence.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 27 and 28

set2.io: 3 — Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology, including genomic epidemiology
set2.q: Pathogens from cases in two different cities turn out to be closely related genetically. What does genomic epidemiology suggest?
opts: The cases may belong to one outbreak
Correct: if pathogens in different cases are closely related, they may be part of the same outbreak; genomic epidemiology links cases in different locations.
The cases must be unrelated
Close genetic relatedness points toward a link, not away from it; it suggests the cases may be part of the same outbreak.
The disease must be inherited
The genes compared are the pathogen's, not the patients'; closely related pathogens suggest the cases may share one outbreak.
The pathogen must be a new species
Relatedness says nothing about a new species; it suggests the cases in different places may belong to the same outbreak.

mis.The disease must be inherited: human genetics confused with pathogen genomics

set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 12 and 69

set2.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set2.q: What is the first step of the policy cycle?
opts: Policy evaluation
Evaluation, collecting data on results, is the fifth and last step.
Assessment of population health
Correct: the cycle runs assessment of population health, assessment of potential interventions, policy choices, policy implementation and policy evaluation.
Assessment of potential interventions
Assessing interventions is the second step, after the issue affecting population health has been identified.
Policy implementation
Implementation, setting target goals and allocating resources, is the fourth step.

set2.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set2.q: Which type of surveillance is the most common, but is less comprehensive and may lead to under-reporting?
opts: Passive surveillance
Correct: passive surveillance relies on reports submitted by facilities and providers; it is the most common type, its data quality is hard to control, and it may under-report.
Active surveillance
Active surveillance, with staff contacting providers, is the most accurate and the most expensive, not the most common.
Sentinel surveillance
Sentinel surveillance uses a smaller prearranged representative group; the most common, under-reporting type is passive surveillance.
Social media monitoring
Social media can be a valuable data source for outbreaks and mental health issues; the most common type is passive surveillance.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 19 and 20

set2.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set2.q: In the investigation of the 1976 Legionnaires' disease epidemic, which study design showed that time spent in one hotel's lobby was a risk factor?
opts: Genomic sequencing
Genomic epidemiology developed much later with sequencing advances; the lobby risk factor came from a case-control study.
Case-control study
Correct: five months after the first cases, the results of a case-control study showed that spending time in the lobby of Hotel A was a risk factor for illness.
Cross-sectional survey
A cross-sectional survey, the community health survey, is a descriptive design; the lobby risk factor came from a case-control study, an analytic design.
Spot map of cases
A spot map plots where cases lived and worked, a descriptive tool; the lobby finding came from a case-control study.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 32 and 67

set2.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set2.q: When epidemiology is applied to a noncommunicable disease, what is the first step?
opts: Define the population of interest
Correct: the steps begin by defining the population of interest, then creating measures of exposure and health indicators, sampling, estimating associations and evaluating causality.
Take a sample of the population
Sampling comes after defining the population and creating measures of exposures and health indicators.
Estimate measures of association
Estimating associations comes after the population is defined, measures created and a sample taken.
Assess external validity
Assessing whether results apply to other populations is the last step; the first is defining the population of interest.

set2.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set2.q: As testing of mild cases expands during an outbreak, what tends to happen to the case fatality rate?
opts: It is underestimated

Correct: the case fatality rate may be overestimated at first, when the sickest cases are hospitalized, and then underestimated as testing of mild cases increases; a long time to resolution can also make it look better than it is.
It is overestimated
Overestimation is the early problem, when the sickest cases are the ones hospitalized and counted; wider testing of mild cases pushes the estimate down.
It becomes exact
More testing does not make it exact; adding many mild cases to the denominator tends to underestimate it.
It is no longer defined
It is still deaths over total cases; adding mild cases to the denominator tends to make it an underestimate.

mis.It becomes exact: belief that more data removes bias

set2.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set2.q: Which of Hill's criteria asks that the proposed causal mechanism make biological sense?
opts: Consistency
Consistency is the same finding across studies and populations; a mechanism that makes biological sense is plausibility.
Biological plausibility
Correct: biological plausibility asks that the proposed causal mechanism be biologically plausible, though the relationship may be indirect and data may not yet support it directly.
Biological gradient
Biological gradient is a dose-response trend; a mechanism that makes biological sense is plausibility.
Specificity
Specificity is an exposure leading to a single or characteristic effect; a sensible mechanism is plausibility.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 46 and 51

set2.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set2.q: Why does timeliness matter in public health surveillance?
opts: So that persons without disease are excluded
Excluding persons without disease is specificity; timeliness is about implementing effective control measures.
So the data collection has legal authority
Legal authority is a planning consideration of its own; timeliness matters so control measures can be implemented effectively.
So control measures can work in time
Correct: timeliness is a critical characteristic because it allows effective control measures to be implemented.
So the temporal trend is pictured accurately
An accurate picture of the temporal trend is what representation provides; timeliness lets control measures work.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 15 and 16
